rationale: PGS001268 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.7346 and PGS-only R²=0.10232 (plus incremental AUROC), whereas PGS002089 provides no PRS-only AUC/R² and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0919), which is harder to interpret for discrimination. Both map to ankylosing spondylitis (same trait_efo), but PGS002089 has slightly cleaner endpoint wording (non–time-to-event) while PGS001268 is time-to-event; this endpoint penalty is outweighed by PGS001268’s much clearer PRS-only metrics and basic covariate set. Although both come from UKB framework-style papers, PGS001268’s evidence package is more directly comparable for PRS quality than PGS002089’s missing PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = abdominal aortic aneurysm; same method PRS-CS; same variant count; same GWAS/EVAL ancestry context and same publication family), so endpoint fidelity and structural properties do not differentiate them. The main visible difference is evaluation packaging: PGS003973 reports a time-to-event discrimination metric (C-index 0.882 with CI) with only basic demographic covariates (Age, Age^2, Sex), which is a cleaner and more interpretable full-model metric than PGS003972’s AUROC 0.69 with covariates listed as Unknown. Neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot credit PRS-only performance; given that, the clearer covariate disclosure and stronger, well-specified discrimination evidence favor PGS003973 over PGS003972.

PGS002755 is the stronger-supported atopic eczema PRS because it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and is evaluated at large scale (EUR eval n=337,910) on an endpoint aligned to the target disease (incident atopic dermatitis/atopic eczema), with only general covariates (age/sex plus socioeconomic/lifestyle). In contrast, PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype (moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis) and its only reported discrimination is a very high AUROC/R² that appears to be full-model (not PGS-only) and is therefore not comparable for PRS ranking; it also uses a very sparse 25-variant score and includes parental ethnicity covariates, with much smaller validation (n=676). With both lacking PRS-only AUC/R², the structural evidence (method + variant coverage) and cleaner interpretability favor PGS002755.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported=incident atopic dermatitis) and use essentially the same covariates and the same EUR evaluation sample size (n=337,910), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. With metrics largely non-comparable, structural signals dominate: PGS002755 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is generally better suited to a polygenic trait like atopic eczema than PGS004587’s 23 genome-wide significant SNP score. The HR separation is also slightly stronger for PGS002755 (1.249 vs 1.153). PGS004587’s listed multi-cohort training sources are a plus, but without PRS-only metrics they don’t outweigh the much stronger genome-wide model structure and slightly stronger effect size in PGS002755.

PGS001135 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (AUROC=0.539 and R2=0.00291 with no covariates) and incremental AUROC, allowing a clean read of PRS contribution and a sanity check against the arthritis heritability ceiling. It also uses only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array) and has multi-ancestry evaluation listed. In contrast, PGS004547 has no AUC/R2/PGS-only metrics at all (only an OR=1.26, which is weak-to-moderate), unknown covariates, and EUR-only evaluation; despite its larger variant count and disease/metaPRS framing, the missing comparable performance fields make it less well-supported for selection here.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUCs are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. However, PGS005168’s reported performance is explicitly packaged with a named clinical risk calculator covariate (CHARGE-AF) alongside age/sex/etc., making its high C-index (0.8718) likely covariate-driven and weak evidence for standalone PRS quality. In contrast, PGS002814 uses only basic covariates (age, sex, top 20 PCs) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.94), which is more interpretable as PRS signal under the provided guidance. Despite PGS005168 having a more genome-wide shrinkage method and many more variants, the CHARGE-AF packaging is a strong negative comparability signal, so PGS002814 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait aortic stenosis: its trait_reported/trait_efo are directly aortic stenosis, whereas PGS005255 is primarily a related quantitative trait (mean pressure gradient) with a broader/mixed trait_efo. Both use the same method (PRS-CS), same EUR-only development/evaluation, identical covariates, identical incident aortic stenosis phenotyping for evaluation, and the same validation sample size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. With metrics missing, the available discriminative evidence favors PGS005254 via a higher per-SD HR (1.64 vs 1.53) and it also has a larger training sample (205,483 vs 98,645), making it the stronger overall package.

PGS001135 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.539) and PGS-only R² (0.00291) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), allowing a clean sanity check against the arthritis heritability ceiling and indicating modest but quantified PRS signal. It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) than PGS004477. In contrast, PGS004477 has no AUROC/R² reported at all (only an OR=1.20, which suggests weak PRS discrimination) and has unknown covariates, reducing comparability; its endpoint is also narrower/administrative (“M13 Other arthritis”) versus the more generic arthritis NOS in PGS001135. While PGS001135 comes from a pan-trait UKB framework (a negative), the lack of comparable performance metrics and weak effect size in PGS004477 leaves it less well-supported overall.

Both candidates match the target trait well (same trait_reported/trait_efo), but PGS003973 has stronger structural and study-support signals: it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1.12M variants and is developed from a large multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis context (many listed cohorts), whereas PGS000753 is a sparse P+T score with only 29 variants and a smaller, older development setup. Neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS003973’s reported C-index=0.882 is a full-model metric (age/age^2/sex) and cannot be treated as PRS-only; however PGS000753’s only comparable performance evidence is a moderate OR=1.37 per SD. Endpoint fidelity is slightly cleaner for PGS003973 (generic AAA vs PGS000753’s explicitly prevalent AAA), and evaluation ancestry is EUR-only for PGS003973 vs mixed AFR/EUR for PGS000753. Overall, the genome-wide method/variant coverage and broader disease-focused development evidence favor PGS003973.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported/phenotyped trait (M13 Other arthritis), same EFO (arthritis), same training cohort (UKB), same training N (174,489), same EUR-only dev/eval ancestry, same variant count (1,059,939), same validation N (56,192), and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (no pgs_only_auc/pgs_only_r2). With metrics missing, the main differentiator is the available effect size: PGS004547 reports a higher per-SD OR (1.262) than PGS004477 (1.196), indicating stronger PRS signal in the visible evidence. Method-wise, PGS004547’s RFDiseasemetaPRS suggests multi-score aggregation, which is a positive structural signal versus the single-score LDpred2 in PGS004477, reinforcing the choice.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and have unknown covariates, so performance must be judged mainly from effect sizes and structural signals. PGS002738 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with far broader variant coverage (326,000 vs 858 for PGS002739) and shows a stronger reported discrimination proxy (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 [1.54–2.51] vs 1.76 [1.32–2.34]). PGS002739 is tailored to African American evaluation (AFR 100% eval) and uses PRS-CSx gene-based, but its much sparser construction and weaker OR provide less direct support on the visible fields. Given the target trait is not ancestry-specified, the stronger overall PRS signal and genome-wide coverage favor PGS002738.

PGS004587 is the better-supported match to the target trait (atopic eczema) because its endpoint is a generic atopic dermatitis diagnosis framed as incident disease (phenotyping_reported: "Incident atopic dermatitis"), aligning well with the broad target concept, whereas PGS001773 targets a narrower severity subtype ("Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis"), which is a partial endpoint mismatch for generic atopic eczema risk. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS001773’s reported AUROC=0.93 and R²=0.49 are full-model metrics (not PRS-comparable) and are therefore not strong evidence of PRS quality, while PGS004587 at least provides a PRS-stratified effect size (HR high vs low PRS = 1.153). Transportability also favors PGS004587 for typical use: it is developed/validated in EUR with very large evaluation (n=337,910), while PGS001773 is MAE-only (Canadian cohorts) with small validation (n=676) and includes parental ethnicity covariates that can complicate comparability. Overall, PGS004587 has cleaner trait alignment and more credible standalone PRS evidence on the visible fields.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to ankylosing spondylitis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and use only basic demographic/PC-style covariates. The key differentiator is performance evidence: PGS001267 reports explicit PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.7265 and PGS-only R2=0.0988 in Europeans), whereas PGS002089 provides no PRS-only AUROC/R2 and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0919), which is less directly comparable for PRS discrimination. Although PGS002089 uses many more variants (22,026) and a genome-wide shrinkage method and has some multi-ancestry evaluation, the absence of standard PRS-only AUC/R2 makes its support weaker on the visible fields than PGS001267’s clearly reported PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUC/C-index is not a comparable PRS metric. PGS005168 is heavily packaged with a named clinical risk calculator covariate (CHARGE-AF) in addition to age/sex/array, making its very high C-index (0.8718) likely covariate-driven and less informative for standalone PRS quality. PGS005313 uses only basic covariates (age, sex), avoiding that risk-wrapper leakage, and it provides a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.82) plus a much larger genome-wide variant set (1,271,239 vs 382,963), which is supportive under the ‘no PGS-only metrics’ fallback. Net: PGS005313 has cleaner comparability and stronger structural/effect-size evidence than the CHARGE-AF–augmented PGS005168.

PGS001267 is the better match to the target trait as a generic ankylosing spondylitis diagnosis endpoint (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both "Ankylosing spondylitis"), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly a time-to-event formulation (trait_reported "Ankylosing spondylitis (time-to-event)"; phenotyping_reported "TTE ankylosing spondylitis"), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic disease target. Both are near-clones otherwise (same pan-trait UKB framework publication, same snpnet method, 10 variants, same training N, same covariates, same ancestry distribution and validation size). Although PGS001268 has slightly higher PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.7346 vs 0.7265; PGS-only R2 0.1023 vs 0.0988), the differences are small and do not outweigh the cleaner endpoint alignment of PGS001267.

PGS002738 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is directly aligned: trait_efo is exactly "alcohol dependence" and both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are "Alcohol use disorder" (a close clinical synonym/umbrella for dependence). It also shows a stronger discrimination signal via an OR(top 10% vs rest)=1.96 (1.54–2.51), which is meaningful effect-size evidence even without PRS-only AUC/R2. In contrast, PGS000201 is less endpoint-faithful (trait_reported "Problematic alcohol use" and trait_efo "alcohol dependence measurement" with a DSM-5 criteria count phenotype), and its only PRS-comparable metric is a small incremental ΔR²=0.01192; while it has explicit basic covariates and more variants, that does not outweigh the weaker phenotype alignment and weaker effect-size/impact evidence for dependence as a disease endpoint.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo are identical). On endpoint fidelity, PGS000753 is slightly less ideal because it is explicitly "Prevalent abdominal aortic aneurysm" whereas PGS003972 is a generic AAA endpoint. Neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS003972’s reported AUROC=0.69 is a full-model metric and cannot be treated as PRS-comparable; however PGS000753 at least reports a PRS effect size (OR=1.37 per SD), indicating moderate PRS signal. The deciding factor is structural/study support: PGS003972 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1.1M variants developed from a large multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis (many cohorts listed; multi-ancestry GWAS), which is generally better-supported than PGS000753’s very sparse 29-variant P+T score from a smaller training set. Covariates are basic/clean for PGS000753 (age/sex/PCs) but unknown for PGS003972; this lowers confidence but is not enough to outweigh the much stronger genome-wide construction and broader disease-focused development context of PGS003972.

PGS002739 is the better-supported match to the target trait (alcohol dependence) because its endpoint is directly aligned: trait_reported="Alcohol use disorder", trait_efo="alcohol dependence", and phenotyping_reported="Alcohol use disorder". It also provides clearer PRS discrimination evidence via an OR (top 10% vs rest)=1.76 (with CI), which is a meaningful effect-size signal when PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent. In contrast, PGS000201 is more weakly aligned (trait_reported="Problematic alcohol use" and trait_efo="alcohol dependence measurement" with a DSM-5 criteria count phenotype rather than a direct AUD case definition) and its only comparable performance signal is a small ΔR²=0.01192 (plus a beta), offering less direct evidence of risk stratification. Confidence is moderated because PGS002739 has covariates listed as unknown and is evaluated only in AFR ancestry, while PGS000201 has explicitly clean/basic covariates and EUR evaluation.

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): its trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are directly aligned to incident aortic stenosis, whereas PGS005255 is primarily a valve-function quantitative trait score (trait_reported="Mean pressure gradient"; trait_efo includes "aortic measurement"), making endpoint fidelity weaker despite mentioning incident AS in phenotyping_reported. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on secondary evidence: PGS005252 shows a stronger per-SD effect size (HR 1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005255), supporting greater PRS signal. PGS005252’s reported C-index=0.87 is full-model and covariate-inflated (many clinical covariates), so it can’t be used as PRS-comparable discrimination, but it still provides more performance context than PGS005255 (which has no AUC/C-index reported). Ancestry is identical (EUR-only) and variant counts are similar, so they don’t differentiate.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo are aortic stenosis; both use incident aortic stenosis phenotyping; both DEV/EVAL EUR only) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must rely on effect-size evidence and comparability signals. PGS005254 has a larger training sample (n=205,483 vs 47,691) and reports an HR per SD of 1.64 with CI (1.50–1.78), giving clearer, more interpretable PRS discrimination evidence than PGS005252’s HR=1.92 without CI. PGS005252’s only discrimination-like metric is a full-model C-index=0.87 alongside a very heavy clinical covariate set (multiple comorbidities and BMI/smoking/renal failure), which is likely covariate-driven and not PRS-comparable; PGS005254 uses only basic demographic/PC covariates, making its reported HR more attributable to the PRS. Variant counts and ancestry are essentially tied, so the cleaner covariate context and better-supported effect-size reporting favor PGS005254.

PGS001263 is the better-supported choice for the specific target trait atrial flutter because it has exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Atrial flutter”) and it reports PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R²=0.025), which can be sanity-checked against the provided heritability ceiling context. In contrast, PGS002050 targets a broader combined phenotype (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”) rather than flutter alone and lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² entirely (only partial correlation is reported), making its predictive evidence less directly comparable for this head-to-head despite its larger variant count and training N.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the visible AUROC values are full-model and not directly comparable as PRS metrics. With that limitation, PGS005313 has stronger structural support for capturing polygenic signal (PRS-CSx with ~1.27M variants vs PGS002814 P+T with 4,520 variants) and broader GWAS ancestry composition plus multi-ancestry evaluation, suggesting better transportability than PGS002814’s MAE-only development and EAS-only evaluation. Covariates are similarly light (age/sex; PGS002814 adds PCs), and effect sizes are both strong (OR 1.82 vs 1.94), so the method/coverage and evaluation breadth tilt the balance to PGS005313.

Both candidates align to the target (trait_efo includes atrial flutter; both report atrial fibrillation and flutter), but PGS001339 provides cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.613 and PGS-only R2=0.02447 (and incremental AUROC reported), which can be sanity-checked against the provided heritability ceiling context. PGS002050 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 entirely and reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.1034), which is less directly comparable for PRS discrimination. Covariates are basic in both (no obvious clinical leakage), and ancestry evaluation breadth is similar; although PGS002050 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many more variants, the absence of PRS-comparable metrics makes it less well-supported on the visible fields than PGS001339.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly “Bipolar disorder/bipolar disorder,” whereas PGS002787 is explicitly subtype-restricted (“Type 1 bipolar disorder” / “bipolar I disorder”), which is a narrower endpoint than the target. Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same publication, SDPR method, PGC training cohort, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, basic covariates age+PCs1-3, no PGS-only AUC/R2; only small full-model partial R² differences that are not decisive). Given the lack of PRS-comparable metrics and the non-disease phenotyping_reported fields in both records, the decision rests mainly on endpoint fidelity, favoring PGS002786.

PGS001263 is the better match to the target trait (atrial flutter) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all specifically “Atrial flutter,” whereas PGS001339 is a combined endpoint (“atrial fibrillation and flutter”) and explicitly time-to-event (phenotyping_reported: “TTE atrial fibrillation and flutter”), which is a weaker endpoint-fidelity match for a generic atrial flutter target. Both are from the same pan-trait UKB snpnet framework paper with identical training size (n=269,704), similar variant counts (2087 vs 2142), same basic covariates, and same validation size (n=24,905), so performance is the main secondary differentiator; PGS001263 is also marginally higher on PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.61716 vs 0.613; PGS-only R2 0.02517 vs 0.02447), with both well below the heritability ceiling sanity check. Net: better phenotype alignment plus slightly better PRS-only metrics for PGS001263.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (basal cell carcinoma), same EUR-only ancestry across GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI) and training N (11,734), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same validation N (11,322), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC ~0.632). With endpoint fidelity and study context indistinguishable, the only visible differentiator is slightly stronger performance in PGS000454: marginally higher Nagelkerke pseudo-R² (0.0489 vs 0.0487) and higher top-1% vs rest OR (3.79 vs 3.61), while AUROC and per-SD OR are essentially the same. Given the tiny metric differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, confidence is low.

Both candidates have identical endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all basal cell carcinoma), similar basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PC1-4), same EUR-only context, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not PRS-comparable). With metrics largely non-comparable, PGS000452 has slightly stronger supporting evidence on the visible record: it reports additional calibration/discrimination-related metrics (Nagelkerke pseudo-R², Brier score, and OR top 1% vs rest) alongside a similar per-SD OR (1.663 vs 1.65 for PGS000119). PGS000119’s marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.64 vs 0.632) and larger validation N are weak differentiators here. Overall this is near-tied, hence low confidence.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Breast cancer/breast carcinoma), identical training cohort and size (UKB; n=12,483), identical evaluation ancestry mix (EUR/SAS) and validation sample size (n=48,968), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R² shown, so differences are weak). Given that, PGS004153 is preferred because it is a MultiPRS ensemble (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV), which is a positive structural signal versus the single-score LDpred2.CV in PGS004040, and it also shows slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.6625 vs 0.6598) and OR per SD (1.826 vs 1.809), albeit small. With near-clone metadata and no PRS-only metrics, confidence is moderate rather than high.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002788 targets the subtype bipolar II disorder (type 2), which is a narrower endpoint mismatch for a generic bipolar disorder target. Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same publication, SDPR method, PGC training cohort, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, same covariates age+PCs1-3, same validation n=2,524) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; the only metric shown is a small partial R² (full-model) that is not PRS-comparable and differs only trivially (0.00251 vs 0.00307), so it should not override endpoint fidelity. Therefore the exact endpoint alignment of PGS002786 makes it the stronger-supported choice.

Both candidates are near-clones in study context (same publication, SDPR method, PGC training cohort, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, basic covariates age+PCs1-3) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R²—only small partial R² values that are not clearly PRS-comparable. Endpoint fidelity to the target trait “bipolar disorder” slightly favors PGS002787 because its mapped trait is bipolar I disorder (Type 1), which is closer to the generic bipolar disorder umbrella than PGS002788’s bipolar II disorder (Type 2). Although PGS002788 has a marginally higher partial R² (0.00307 vs 0.00275) and slightly larger validation n (2,524 vs 2,198), these differences are small and the phenotyping_reported fields for both look behavior/proxy-like rather than direct bipolar diagnosis, so the decision rests mainly on the closer trait alignment of PGS002787.

PGS000327 has strong endpoint fidelity: trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to “Autism spectrum disorder,” whereas PGS002790’s phenotyping_reported is explicitly mismatched (“Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)”), a major penalty per the endpoint-fidelity guidance. On performance evidence, neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², but PGS000327 provides supportive effect-size evidence (OR=1.33 per SD) and a higher reported R² (0.0245) than PGS002790’s partial R² (0.00546), with both well below the ASD heritability ceiling. PGS000327 also has clearer disease-focused development metadata (multi-cohort ASD GWAS paper; training n=28,592; validation n=7,148) versus PGS002790 with N/A training size and a smaller validation (n=2,198). Despite PGS002790 using a genome-wide shrinkage method with more variants, the explicit phenotype mismatch and weaker reported signal make PGS000327 better supported overall.

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to breast cancer/breast carcinoma), come from the same publication, have the same training cohort (UKB), training N (12,483), evaluation ancestry mix, and no covariates listed (covariates=0). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use PRS-comparable metrics and must treat the full-model AUROC/R² differences as weak. Given that, PGS004153 has a small but consistent edge over PGS004025 in the selected validation record (higher full-model AUROC 0.6625 vs 0.6598; higher R² 0.0764 vs 0.0736; slightly higher OR per SD 1.826 vs 1.806) and also a modestly higher variant count (1,133,268 vs 1,041,298). These are minor differences, hence moderate confidence, but they favor PGS004153.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to celiac disease (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the visible AUROC values are full-model and not cleanly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. With that limitation, PGS000040 has stronger structural support: a substantially larger variant set (228 vs 53) and a disease-focused statistical learning approach (SparSNP) with a slightly higher reported AUROC (0.90 vs 0.879, though likely not decisive). PGS000316’s main advantage is larger training and much larger validation sample size, but validation N is a weak tie-break and does not compensate for the weaker PRS structure/coverage given the lack of PRS-only metrics in both.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment to basal cell carcinoma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch/PC1-4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported—so full-model AUROC differences (0.632 for PGS000454 vs 0.64 for PGS000119) are not a reliable differentiator. PGS000454 provides a slightly richer and cleaner evidence package on the visible record: it reports additional supporting metrics (Nagelkerke pseudo-R², Brier score, and top-1% vs rest OR=3.79) alongside a comparable per-SD OR (~1.66, similar to PGS000119’s 1.65). PGS000119’s main advantages are marginally higher full-model AUROC and larger validation N, both weak signals here. Hence PGS000454 narrowly wins, but confidence is low due to near-tie and lack of PRS-only metrics in both.

PGS001301 has clearly reported PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.82867 and PGS-only R²=0.14224) with only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), whereas PGS000040 lacks any PGS-only metrics and only shows a full-model AUROC=0.9, which is not a valid substitute for PRS-only discrimination. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (PGS000040: coeliac disease; PGS001301: malabsorption/coeliac disease still explicitly includes coeliac disease), but PGS001301 provides much cleaner, directly comparable evidence of PRS contribution and broader evaluation ancestry reporting. The relatively high PGS-only R² for PGS001301 vs the provided liability h² ceiling warrants some caution, so confidence is not high, but it remains better-supported than PGS000040 given the missing PRS-only metrics.

PGS001301 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.82867; PGS R2(no covariates)=0.14224) with clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs) and includes some non-EUR evaluation (AFR/SAS) in addition to EUR. In contrast, PGS000316 provides only a full-model AUROC (0.879) with covariates listed as unknown and no PGS-only AUC/R2, making its performance less comparable for judging standalone PRS quality despite a disease-focused title and very large evaluation N. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (celiac disease), though PGS001301’s reported phenotype is a broader composite (“Malabsorption/coeliac disease”), so confidence is not high.

Both candidates are near-clones for breast carcinoma: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (Breast cancer), identical variant count (1,041,298), same training cohort (UKB) and training N (12,483), same ancestry distribution (GWAS/DEV EUR; EVAL EUR+SAS) and same validation N (48,968). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R²), so performance evidence is weakly comparable and differences are essentially noise. As a tie-break, PGS004040 has marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.65978971 vs 0.65975886), R² (0.07391539 vs 0.07358668), and OR per SD (1.8088 vs 1.8065) than PGS004025, so it is very slightly better supported on the visible metrics.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo cervical carcinoma; phenotyping is direct cervical cancer). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index is only weakly informative; still, PGS003428 shows stronger discrimination/effect evidence (C-index 0.613; HR per SD 1.33) than PGS005165 (C-index 0.566; HR 1.2). Structurally, PGS003428 is a genome-wide LDpred score with ~2.9M variants from a cervical-phenotype GWAS meta-analysis context, whereas PGS005165 is a 15-SNP genome-wide-significant loci score from a pan-cancer risk paper, which is a weaker archetype for disease-specific PRS quality. Covariates are light in both (age+smoking vs age/region/PCs). Ancestry differs (EUR vs EAS), but with no deployment ancestry specified, the stronger disease-focused, genome-wide model with better effect size support is PGS003428.

Both candidates align well to the target trait (trait_efo cervical carcinoma; trait_reported cervical cancer) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index/AUROC are not clean PRS-comparable differentiators. On the available evidence, PGS000073 has slightly stronger validation discrimination (C-index ~0.75; full-model AUROC 0.745) than PGS005165 (C-index 0.566; full-model AUROC 0.566), with similar per-SD HRs (1.22 vs 1.20). Although PGS000073 uses more epidemiologic covariates (parity, oral contraceptive use, smoking pack-years) than PGS005165’s mostly basic covariates, neither shows heavy clinical leakage (no family history/biomarkers/risk-calculator packaging). Given the materially higher reported discrimination and comparable endpoint fidelity, PGS000073 is better supported overall, but confidence is only moderate because the key metrics are full-model rather than PRS-only and covariate sets differ.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo cervical carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident cervical cancer). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC/C-index in PGS000073 (0.745–0.75) is not a reliable PRS-quality differentiator, especially given its much heavier covariate set (PCs, parity, oral contraceptive use, pack-years, etc.) versus the lighter adjustment in PGS003428 (age, smoking). Structurally, PGS003428 is a genome-wide LDpred score with ~2.9M variants from a cervical-phenotype GWAS meta-analysis context with multiple development cohorts (EB, FinnGen, KP, UKB) and shows a somewhat stronger per-SD effect size (HR 1.33 vs 1.22), whereas PGS000073 is a 10-variant GWAS-hits score from a cross-cancer evaluation framework. Given comparable endpoints but cleaner covariate comparability and stronger disease-focused/genome-wide construction, PGS003428 is better supported overall.

Both candidates target COPD with identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported and come from the same publication using the same method (PRS-CS-auto) with EUR-only evaluation, so endpoint fidelity and study archetype do not differentiate them. The key differentiator is PRS-comparable performance: PGS001783 reports a substantially higher covariates-regressed-out (PGS-only) Nagelkerke R2 (0.038092) than PGS001788 (0.0163), and this is within the trait heritability ceiling guidance. PGS001788 has a much larger validation sample size and slightly more variants, but validation N is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the materially stronger PRS-only R2 signal in PGS001783; additionally PGS001788 uses a more complex covariate set, making its full-model AUROC less comparable.

Both candidates target the exact same endpoint (ICD10 K80 cholelithiasis), same EFO mapping, same training cohort (UKB), same EUR-only development/evaluation, same variant count, and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only OR per SD). With metrics otherwise near-cloned, the main differentiator is the available effect size and model structure: PGS004546 (RFDiseasemetaPRS) shows a higher OR (1.299) than PGS004476 (LDpred2; OR 1.219), indicating stronger PRS signal on the visible record. Given missing PGS-only AUC/R2 and unknown covariates for both, confidence is moderate rather than high.

Both candidates align to cholelithiasis (EFO match). PGS004476 has an ICD10 K80 endpoint (good fidelity) and a genome-wide LDpred2 build with many variants, but it provides no PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUC/R2 are all null) and only a modest OR per SD (~1.22), limiting evidence strength. PGS001174 is from a pan-trait UKB framework (a negative signal) and uses a time-to-event phenotype (some endpoint penalty), but it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.623 and PGS R2 0.028 with basic covariates) that are sanity-consistent with the trait’s h2_obs (~0.021) and offers broader evaluation ancestries. Given the absence of comparable metrics for PGS004476, the better-supported record on visible evidence is PGS001174.

PGS001174 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.623 and PGS-only R²=0.028 (both interpretable and broadly consistent with the trait’s low observed h² ceiling), with clearly stated basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array). It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), supporting transportability. In contrast, PGS004546 has good endpoint fidelity (ICD10 K80) and a moderate OR per SD (~1.30), but provides no PRS-only AUROC/R² (only an effect size) and has unknown covariates, making its predictive performance and comparability less well evidenced from the visible fields.

ontology: congenital vitamin k-dependent coagulation factors deficiency
rationale: Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), identical training cohort and size (UKB; n=391,124), identical covariates, identical ancestry distribution and validation size, and essentially identical PRS-comparable performance evidence (partial-r 0.0563 for PGS002034 vs 0.0562 for PGS001826 with overlapping CIs). With metrics and phenotype tied, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002034 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (32,552 vs 45), which is generally a positive signal for capturing polygenic signal when other evidence is indistinguishable. The advantage is small given near-identical partial-r, hence moderate confidence.

Both candidates target the exact same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all corneal dystrophy), come from the same UKB portability publication, have identical training size, covariates, ancestry distribution, and validation sample size—so the decision rests on the limited performance and structural signals available. PGS002042 shows higher PRS-comparable performance in the selected record (partial-r 0.0471 vs 0.0384 for PGS001835) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far broader variant coverage (59,944 vs 38 variants), which is generally a positive structural indicator when endpoints are identical. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, the partial-r advantage plus much larger variant set makes PGS002042 better supported.

PGS002237 has tighter endpoint fidelity via an explicit phenotype definition for CKD stage ≥3 (eGFR <45 ml/min/1.73m2) and shows broader external evaluation across multiple ancestries (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE), supporting transportability for the generic target “chronic kidney disease.” PGS005090 is also stage ≥3 but its phenotyping is vague (“Chronic kidney disease”) and its evidence is confined to AFR-only GWAS/EVAL; its very high reported AUROC=0.90 is a full-model metric (no PGS-only AUC/R2) and thus not comparable, especially given differing covariate sets. With both lacking PRS-only metrics, the clearer phenotype specification and multi-ancestry validation breadth make PGS002237 better-supported overall.

PGS001783 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance and structural plausibility for COPD: it reports a covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.038092, which aligns closely with the provided COPD heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0388) and is far stronger than PGS001332’s PGS-only R2=0.00235 and PGS-only AUROC=0.53971. Endpoint fidelity is essentially equivalent (both map to COPD; PGS001332’s phenotyping is a near-synonym ‘chronic obstructive airways disease/copd’). While PGS001332 has larger training/validation and multi-ancestry evaluation, it comes from the ‘813 traits’ sparse UKB framework (snpnet, 482 variants) which is explicitly a weaker archetype for external generalization than the global multi-biobank PRS-CS-auto genome-wide score in PGS001783 (884,139 variants, many contributing cohorts). PGS001783 lacks a PGS-only AUROC, lowering confidence, but its much higher PRS-only R2 and stronger study/method structure outweigh PGS001332’s modest PGS-only AUROC.

Both candidates match the target CAD endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all coronary artery disease) and both use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS000013 also adds chip). The key difference is evidence of PRS strength and transportability: PGS003725 is from a CAD-focused multi-ancestry PRS study and shows strong PRS effect sizes (HR 1.75 and OR 2.14 per SD), with explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/MAE/SAS), supporting robustness beyond EUR. PGS000013 provides a PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only R2=0.04, below the heritability ceiling) but its prominent AUROC=0.81 is full-model (not PRS-only) and thus not comparable; it also lacks effect-size evidence here. Given PGS003725’s stronger PRS-specific effect-size signal plus broader evaluation ancestry in a disease-focused context, it is better-supported overall despite missing explicit PGS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Cirrhosis/cirrhosis of liver”) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC cannot be used as a clean PRS discriminator. Given that, PGS004621 has stronger structural and study-design support: a genome-wide shrinkage PRS-CS model with ~1.09M variants and very large European validation (n=1,153,995) across many biobanks, with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs). PGS000726 is a much sparser 12-variant GWS score with smaller validation (n=30,469) and its stronger reported contrast OR (top 20% vs bottom 20% = 2.26) is supportive but not directly comparable to per-SD effects; overall the sparse construction provides weaker evidence of capturing polygenic signal for cirrhosis than the genome-wide PRS-CS approach in PGS004621.

Both candidates align well to the target COPD concept (trait_reported/trait_efo match), but PGS001788 has cleaner and stronger PRS-comparable evidence: it reports a covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.0163, which is materially higher than PGS001332’s PGS R2 (no covariates)=0.00235 and remains below the provided COPD h2_obs ceiling (~0.0122) in the expected range (whereas PGS001332’s headline AUROC advantage is largely full-model/covariate-driven, with only PGS-only AUROC=0.5397). Structurally and transport-wise, PGS001788 is a genome-wide shrinkage score (PRS-CS-auto) with ~910k variants and multi-biobank development plus very large EUR evaluation (n=337,168), while PGS001332 is a very sparse snpnet score (482 variants) from the pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ framework, which domain guidance flags as systematically weaker for external generalization. PGS001332 does have multi-ancestry evaluation listed, but its PRS-only metrics are weak; overall support favors PGS001788.

PGS002237 has tighter endpoint fidelity to generic chronic kidney disease: it targets CKD stage ≥3 with an explicit eGFR<45 definition, whereas PGS004889 uses a restricted phenotype (“incident CKD cases without diabetes”), which is a narrower, conditioned endpoint and less aligned to the broad target trait. Neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model discrimination ~0.78), so performance metrics are not cleanly comparable; in that setting, PGS002237’s stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.47 vs HR 1.30 for PGS004889) is more supportive of PRS signal. PGS004889 also shows heavier clinical packaging in covariates (a combined clinical risk score from BP/weight/HTN history), making its full-model C-index less informative about the PRS itself compared with PGS002237’s more standard epidemiologic covariate set.

PGS004621 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are directly “Cirrhosis/cirrhosis of liver,” whereas PGS000704 is explicitly restricted to “Alcoholic cirrhosis” (trait_efo: alcoholic liver cirrhosis), a subtype/exposure-specific endpoint that is a weaker fidelity match for a generic cirrhosis target. Neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC/C-index values (0.68 vs 0.711) are not cleanly comparable; in that setting, PGS004621’s stronger PRS effect size signal (OR 1.42 vs HR 1.18 for PGS000704) and its disease-focused multi-cohort development context (multiple biobanks vs UKB-only) provide more credible support than PGS000704’s modestly higher full-model C-index and larger training N.

PGS005090 is better aligned to the target CKD endpoint: it explicitly targets "Chronic kidney disease (stage 3 or higher)" with phenotyping_reported simply "Chronic kidney disease," whereas PGS004889 restricts to "Incident chronic kidney disease cases without diabetes," a narrower, conditioned phenotype that is less faithful to generic CKD risk. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported full-model AUROC/C-index are not comparable PRS metrics; however, PGS005090 at least reports a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.41) with relatively basic covariates (age, sex, diabetes, PCs), while PGS004889 uses heavier clinical packaging (diagnosis history plus BP/weight and an HTN clinical risk score), making its C-index (0.78) more covariate-driven and less informative about the PRS itself. Ancestry-wise, PGS005090 is coherently developed/evaluated in AFR (African American) with large validation (n=67,819), while PGS004889’s mixed-ancestry development/evaluation context plus phenotype restriction adds uncertainty for general CKD deployment.

Both candidates match the target CAD endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Coronary artery disease”), use the same method (LDpred), have nearly identical variant counts (~6.6M), and similarly basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS000013 also lists chip). The key differentiator is comparable PRS performance evidence: PGS000013 reports a PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2=0.04 / Nagelkerke R2=0.04), which is interpretable and below the provided CAD heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.13), whereas PGS002244 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 at all (only an OR=1.64). Although PGS002244 has a larger training and validation sample and a strong OR, the absence of PRS-comparable metrics makes it less directly supported on the visible fields than PGS000013.

Both candidates are well-aligned to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Coronary artery disease”) and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so the decision leans on effect-size evidence, covariate cleanliness, and study/transportability context. PGS003725 shows stronger discriminative signal via larger per-SD effect sizes (OR 2.14 and HR 1.75) than PGS002244 (OR 1.64 only), with similarly basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS002244 adds possible dataset-specific technical covariates but no clear clinical leakage). While PGS002244 has broader GWAS ancestry mix and more variants, and slightly larger training/validation N, those are weaker differentiators here than the materially stronger OR/HR evidence in PGS003725 given both are endpoint-faithful and metric-limited.

PGS005170 is the better-supported match to the target trait dementia because its reported trait and EFO mapping align directly to dementia ("All-cause dementia"; trait_efo="dementia") with the same phenotyping endpoint (incident all-cause dementia), whereas PGS000823 is primarily an Alzheimer’s disease score (trait_efo="Alzheimer disease"), making it a narrower/partially mismatched concept for an all-cause dementia target despite similar phenotyping text. Neither record provides PRS-comparable PGS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be cleanly compared; however PGS005170 at least reports an HR per SD (1.25) and is structurally a large, genome-wide integrative/ensemble score (1,320,229 variants) with multi-ancestry evaluation listed, while PGS000823 is a 23-variant genome-wide-significant score with only a coarse HR contrast metric and EUR-only evaluation. PGS005170’s covariates include APOE alleles (some packaging/augmentation risk), but PGS000823’s simpler covariates don’t compensate for the weaker endpoint fidelity and much sparser genetic model.

Both candidates map to Alzheimer’s disease (trait_reported/trait_efo) and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so we rely on endpoint fidelity, covariate cleanliness, and structural signals. PGS002249 aligns better to the target trait dementia via phenotyping_reported="Incident dementia" and shows a stronger reported genetic-risk separation (HR 1.91 high vs low) than PGS000823 (HR 1.36 top vs bottom tertile), consistent with a more informative PRS signal. Although PGS002249 uses heavier covariates (education, socioeconomic status, lifestyle categories) than PGS000823 (age, sex only), the absence of PRS-only metrics in both means the stronger effect-size evidence plus much more polygenic construction (249,273 variants vs 23) makes PGS002249 better-supported overall for dementia risk.

PGS004862 is preferred because it is the MTAG-enhanced version of the same dilated cardiomyopathy endpoint (trait_reported: "Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)" vs PGS004861 "Dilated cardiomyopathy"), and domain guidance explicitly states MTAG variants from the same study family are mildly preferred as legitimate power-boosted enhancements. Endpoint fidelity is otherwise identical (same trait_efo, phenotyping_reported, covariates, ancestry, cohorts, and validation n). With no PGS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, we fall back to the available within-family signals: PGS004862 shows slightly stronger reported full-model metrics and effect size (AUROC 0.71 vs 0.70; R² 0.05 vs 0.048; OR 1.76 vs 1.56), while variant counts are essentially tied. Differences are modest, so confidence is moderate.

PGS000726 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_efo is exactly "cirrhosis of liver" and phenotyping_reported is the generic diagnosis "Cirrhosis," whereas PGS000704 is explicitly restricted to the subtype "Alcoholic cirrhosis" (trait_efo "alcoholic liver cirrhosis"), which is a narrower endpoint and a partial mismatch for a generic cirrhosis target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS000704’s reported C-index=0.711 is a full-model metric and not a clean PRS-comparable advantage; by contrast PGS000726 provides supportive PRS discrimination evidence via effect sizes (OR per SD 1.32; OR top vs bottom quintile 2.26). Study/transportability context also favors PGS000726: it is developed across multiple cohorts/biobanks (ACG, ARIC, BBJ, BioVU, FinnGen, PHB, UKB) with multi-ancestry evaluation listed, while PGS000704 is UKB-only development with EUR/MAE evaluation. Overall, endpoint fidelity plus multi-cohort disease-focused support outweigh PGS000704’s larger variant count and non-PRS full-model C-index.

PGS004951 is better supported for dilated cardiomyopathy because it provides explicit PRS-comparable performance evidence (Univariate/PRS-only AUC=0.67 with CI, plus delta PRS/residual liability-scale R²=0.101), whereas PGS004861 reports only full-model metrics (AUROC=0.70, R²=0.048) that are not directly comparable as standalone PRS performance. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (both map to dilated cardiomyopathy; PGS004951’s “(MTAG)” is not a mismatch and its phenotyping is explicitly clinical), and covariates are basic in both (no obvious leakage). Although PGS004861 has a much larger validation sample (n=347,585 vs n=7,761), validation size is a weak tie-breaker and does not outweigh PGS004951’s clearer PRS-only metrics and stronger effect size (OR 1.93 vs 1.56).

Both candidates are essentially endpoint-identical for dupuytren contracture (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), come from the same UKB portability paper, have the same training size, covariates, ancestry distribution, and validation sample size; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only partial-r). With performance nearly tied (partial-r 0.0797 for PGS002092 vs 0.0783 for PGS001880, overlapping CIs), the main differentiator is structural: PGS002092 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (484,484 vs 2,443), which is generally favored for polygenic traits when other evidence is equal. Hence PGS002092 is slightly better supported, but confidence is only moderate because the empirical metric difference is minimal.

Both candidates align well to the target (same trait_efo Dupuytren Contracture; phenotyping_reported is a direct Dupuytren/palmar fascia contracture endpoint in both). The key differentiator is comparable PRS-only performance evidence: PGS001254 reports explicit PRS-only AUROC=0.6646 and PRS-only R²=0.0247 (with basic covariates), whereas PGS001880 provides no PRS-only AUROC/R² and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0783), which is less directly comparable for PRS discrimination. Although PGS001880 has broader multi-ancestry evaluation and many more variants (2443 vs 11), the absence of standard PRS-only metrics makes its support weaker on the visible fields than PGS001254’s clear PRS-only AUC/R² reporting.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_efo=Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported=lymphocytic thyroiditis), use the same method (PRSCS), have essentially identical variant counts (~1.085M), the same evaluation ancestry mix, and the same validation sample size (n=94,651) with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (only full-model AUROC, which is discounted). Given this, the best differentiator is the available effect-size/performance evidence: PGS005271 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.6297 vs 0.6054) and a stronger per-SD effect (OR 1.55 vs 1.42; beta 0.438 vs 0.349), which supports stronger PRS signal than PGS005272 within the same study family.

Both candidates match the target concept well (trait_reported/trait_efo are identical), but PGS002763 has cleaner endpoint framing for generic hip osteoarthritis risk (phenotyping_reported: "Hip osteoarthritis") versus PGS004882’s explicitly incident/time-to-event endpoint ("Incident hip osteoarthritis"), which is a mild mismatch for a generic disease target. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS004882’s only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index=0.6 (not PRS-comparable), so it cannot be used as evidence of stronger standalone PRS. Effect-size evidence is similar (PGS002763 OR=1.38 vs PGS004882 HR=1.4, both moderate). With performance essentially tied and PGS004882’s metric being non-comparable plus its incident packaging, PGS002763 is better-supported on endpoint fidelity and comparability despite smaller validation size.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (trait_efo) with identical reported/phenotyping labels (“lymphocytic thyroiditis”), same publication family, same evaluation ancestry mix, and same validation sample size (n=94,651). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; the only AUROC shown is full-model and thus not a clean differentiator, especially given unknown covariates for both. In this setting, structural/effect-size evidence matters more: PGS005271 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRS-CS) with 1,085,156 variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.55) than PGS005270’s very weak effect (OR≈1.04) despite PGS005270 having a slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.639 vs 0.630). Therefore PGS005271 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for the target trait.

Both candidates have essentially identical endpoint fidelity for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (trait_efo matches; trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both “Lymphocytic thyroiditis”), same publication family/date, same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and same validation sample size (n=94,651), with covariates unknown in both—so phenotype/transportability do not differentiate. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; the only AUROC shown is full-model and thus weakly comparable. In this no-PRS-only-metrics setting, PGS005272 is better supported structurally and by effect size: it uses PRSCS with genome-wide coverage (1,085,142 variants) and shows a much stronger per-SD OR (~1.42) than PGS005270 (OR ~1.04), whereas the small full-model AUROC difference (0.639 vs 0.605) is not a reliable differentiator. Therefore PGS005272 is the stronger-supported PRS candidate here.

Both candidates are well-aligned to the target (same trait_efo Dupuytren Contracture; phenotyping_reported is a direct Dupuytren/palmar fascia contracture endpoint in both). PGS001254 has cleaner PRS-comparable metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646; PGS-only R2 0.0247), whereas PGS002092 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 and only shows a partial correlation (partial-r 0.0797), so metric evidence favors PGS001254. However, PGS001254 comes from the known pan-trait UKB sparse framework ("across 813 traits", snpnet) with an extremely sparse 11-variant score, which is a portability/generalization warning signal; PGS002092, while also from a UKB portability-style paper, uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with ~484k variants and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), providing stronger structural and transportability support. Given the framework/sparsity penalty and much stronger genome-wide construction, PGS002092 is better-supported overall despite missing PRS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin’s disease/lymphoma), same publication family, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training n=736, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation size (n=775). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use PRS-comparable discrimination and must rely on within-family empirical signals. PGS000639 shows consistently stronger reported performance/effect evidence than PGS000638: higher AUROC in the reported model (0.62 vs 0.601), higher Nagelkerke pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.377), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.62). With endpoint and covariates effectively identical, these stronger metrics make PGS000639 better supported.

Both candidates match the target conceptually (trait_reported/trait_efo are hip osteoarthritis; EUR evaluation). However, PGS002728 comes from a disease-focused osteoarthritis PRS paper and is developed across multiple OA-relevant cohorts (EB, GARP, HUNT, LLS, MyCode, UKB, arcOGEN, deCODE), whereas PGS004882 is from a broad incidence-framework paper and its listed development cohort is just 1000G, which is weaker direct disease-development evidence. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model metrics are discounted; still, PGS002728 shows a slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.66 vs 0.60) with similarly light covariates (age/sex vs PCs). PGS004882 does provide an HR per SD (1.4, moderate), but the framework-style context and incident time-to-event packaging make it less compelling than the multi-cohort disease-focused support for PGS002728.

PGS005170 is the better match to the target trait dementia on endpoint fidelity and model structure: it explicitly targets "All-cause dementia" with phenotyping_reported "Incident all-cause dementia" (directly aligned to the broad dementia target), whereas PGS002249 is an Alzheimer’s disease PRS (trait_efo Alzheimer disease) even though its phenotyping_reported is incident dementia, creating a concept mismatch vs the target. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC in PGS005170 (0.761) cannot be used as a comparable PRS metric; however PGS005170 still has supportive per-SD effect size evidence (HR 1.25) and a stronger structural approach (integrative ensemble of 24 component PRSs; 1.32M variants) compared with PGS002249’s simpler LD clumping score (249k variants) and only a grouped HR (high vs low genetic risk 1.91) that is less directly comparable. PGS005170 also shows broader evaluation ancestry coverage (including AFR/AMR/EAS) than PGS002249 (EUR-only), supporting transportability. Main caveat lowering confidence: PGS005170 adjusts for APOE alleles (potentially soaking up major genetic signal), while PGS002249 includes lifestyle categories (non-genetic packaging), so both have comparability concerns.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo = Hodgkins lymphoma), identical ancestry (EUR-only), same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes (n=736 train; n=775 eval), and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given this near-clone setup, PGS000638 has slightly stronger reported performance/effect evidence in the selected validation record: higher AUROC (0.601 vs 0.574) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0193 vs 0.013) and a slightly higher per-SD OR (1.377 vs 1.30). PGS000637’s genome-wide PRS-CS/large variant count is a structural plus, but within this same-publication, same-endpoint comparison the observed validation metrics favor PGS000638; confidence is low because differences are small and metrics are full-model rather than PRS-only.

PGS004236 is better supported for the target hypertension because it comes from a disease-focused, multi-cohort, explicitly multi-ethnic study (BioMe/MVP/UKB) with multi-ancestry evaluation and reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=2.1), whereas PGS001320 is from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet) that is penalized for weaker real-world transportability despite having clean PGS-only AUROC/R2 (0.629/0.0649). Although PGS004236 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 and only shows a full-model AUROC (0.764) that is not PRS-comparable and uses heavier covariates (including BMI and smoking), its endpoint remains aligned (prevalent hypertension) and the strong OR plus disease-focused multi-cohort design outweigh the framework-origin advantage of PGS001320’s reported PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates target the same trait (Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG); EFO matches) and use the same method (PRS-CS) with broadly comparable, non-leaky covariates (A: age/sex/PCs; B: sex/PCs). The key differentiator is that PGS004951 reports PRS-comparable performance evidence (explicit univariate PRS-only AUC=0.67 with CI and delta PRS/residual liability-scale R²=0.101), whereas PGS004862 provides only full-model AUROC=0.71 and an unlabeled R²=0.05 that are not clearly PRS-only and thus are discounted for PRS comparison. PGS004951 also shows a slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.93 vs 1.76) and has higher variant count, while its smaller validation n is a weak negative. Overall, the cleaner PRS-only metric reporting and stronger effect size make PGS004951 better-supported than PGS004862.

PGS002763 has the cleaner endpoint match to the target trait: phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Hip osteoarthritis,” whereas PGS002728 uses “Total hip replacement,” a treatment/proxy endpoint that can reflect access/clinical decision-making and is less faithful to disease status. Although PGS002728 has a more explicitly disease-focused multi-cohort development list, the endpoint proxy plus lack of PRS-isolated performance makes it less well-supported for ‘hip osteoarthritis’ than PGS002763’s direct phenotype alignment and stronger structural PRS properties.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo: Hodgkins lymphoma), come from the same publication, use the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and have identical EUR-only training/evaluation context and validation size (n=775), so the decision rests on the available performance/effect-size evidence. Performance fields for both are not PRS-comparable (only full-model AUROC shown), but PGS000739’s reported AUROC is additionally confounded by heavy clinical covariates (multiple comorbid risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status), making its discrimination less informative for PRS quality than PGS004911’s basic covariate set (age/sex/PCs). Given similar full-model AUROC (~0.8) and cleaner covariates plus stronger PRS construction, PGS004911 is better-supported.

With endpoint fidelity prioritized and other evidence largely similar, PGS000114 wins despite PGS000325’s larger validation N and slightly higher full-model AUROC.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target hyperthyroidism via the clinically dominant subtype Graves’ disease: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%), same validation sample size (n=94,651), and covariates are unknown for both so performance comparability is equally limited (no PGS-only AUC/R2; only full-model AUROC shown). With endpoint fidelity and study context essentially tied, PGS005265 has slightly stronger visible empirical signals than PGS005266: marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.6652 vs 0.6637) and stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 1.625 vs 1.543; β 0.486 vs 0.434), plus trivially more variants (1,085,173 vs 1,085,170). Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match disorders of iron metabolism), identical training cohort and size (UKB, n=391,124), identical covariates (basic demographics + PCs), identical validation size (n=19,883) and ancestry distribution. The edge is modest, hence moderate confidence.

PGS005266 is better supported for the target hyperthyroidism because its endpoint (Graves’ disease; phenotyping_reported: “graves’ disease”) is a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism and comes from a disease-focused, multi-cohort biobank study with multi-ancestry evaluation (African American/LatAm/European) and a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRSCS, 1,085,170 variants). Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² and reports only a full-model AUROC (0.664), it provides a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.54), which is meaningful PRS evidence. In contrast, PGS001043 has an exact label match (“Hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis”) and clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6323; PGS R² 0.0216), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet) with only 69 variants—an archetype that tends to generalize poorly versus disease-focused multi-cohort scores. Net: stronger study archetype/method/variant coverage and strong OR for PGS005266 outweigh PGS001043’s modest PRS-only metrics from a framework sparse model.

PGS001320 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.629 and PGS-only R²=0.06493 (no covariates), whereas PGS004234 provides no PGS-only AUC/R² and only a full-model AUROC=0.763 that cannot be treated as PRS performance—especially given its heavier covariate set (smoking status, BMI, race/ethnic background, etc.) likely inflating the full-model AUROC. Despite PGS004234 being from a hypertension-focused multi-ethnic study, the lack of PRS-only metrics makes its standalone PRS strength less evidenced than PGS001320’s clearly reported PRS-only discrimination.

PGS005265 is better supported for the target hyperthyroidism because its endpoint (Graves’ disease) is the clinically dominant autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism and is explicitly noted as a strong match in the provided domain guidance, whereas PGS001043 comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank “813 traits” sparse framework that is specifically warned to generalize poorly despite having cleanly reported PRS-only metrics. While PGS001043 does report PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.6323; PGS R2 0.02158, below the heritability ceiling), its evidence is tied to a single-biobank framework design with very few variants (69) and modest PRS-only discrimination; in contrast PGS005265 is a disease-focused multi-cohort/multi-biobank score (many external cohorts listed) using genome-wide shrinkage (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (~1.1M) and a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.63), even though it lacks explicit PGS-only AUROC/R2 and only shows a full-model AUROC. Missing PRS-only metrics for PGS005265 lowers confidence, but the combination of dominant-subtype endpoint fidelity plus disease-focused multi-cohort design outweighs the framework penalty on PGS001043.

Both candidates target the same trait (hypertension; prevalent hypertension), come from the same publication, have identical training N (10,314), validation N (39,035), evaluation ancestry, and the same covariate set (includes BMI/smoking but no obvious high-leakage clinical packaging). PGS004234 lacks effect-size reporting and is a sparser C+T-style construction (PRSice-2) with fewer variants, offering less support given the otherwise near-clone metadata.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target-aligned trait_reported/trait_efo (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease), same phenotyping_reported (familial LOAD), same method (genome-wide significant variants) with the same 21 variants, same covariates (age, sex), and same multi-cohort development context from the same publication. PGS000053 has a larger EUR validation sample (n=4,792 vs n=3,324) and EUR-only evaluation, but validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the much stronger OR signal in PGS000054.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it is disease-focused (multi-ancestry kidney cancer GWAS identifying susceptibility regions) with a direct kidney cancer endpoint (phenotyping_reported: “Kidney cancer”) and shows a much stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD 1.5, 95% CI 1.43–1.58) than PGS000787 (HR 1.15, 1.07–1.24), which suggests weaker standalone discrimination. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown), so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.74 vs 0.722) is not decisive; in that setting, the stronger effect size and richer disease-GWAS basis (107 genome-wide significant SNPs vs 19 variants reused/inverted from another score) favor PGS004908. Both candidates match the target trait well (same trait_efo: late-onset Alzheimer’s disease; phenotyping_reported is direct LOAD in both, with PGS000054 specifying familial late-onset LOAD). PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to the umbrella JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) with phenotyping_reported restricted to that subtype. Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo = lung cancer/carcinoma; phenotyping_reported = incident lung cancer), have identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS and evaluation), identical variant count (109), identical covariate set (including substantial non-genetic risk-factor packaging like smoking variables, PM2.5, and family history), and essentially identical reported discrimination/effect size (full-model AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849; HR per SD ~1.16–1.17). Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo are lung cancer/lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported is incident lung cancer; EUR GWAS/EVAL). Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer; EUR GWAS/EVAL). Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported kidney cancer; trait_efo renal cell carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident kidney cancer), use the same covariates, same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same variant count (19), and show essentially identical full-model discrimination (AUROC ~0.722; C-index ~0.723–0.724) and similar HR per SD (1.16 vs 1.15). Both candidates map cleanly to systemic lupus erythematosus (same trait_reported and trait_efo) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the visible AUROC values are full-model and not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate multiple myeloma / plasma cell myeloma) and both are sparse GWAS-hit style scores with similar variant counts (PGS002306: 23 vs PGS000653: 22) and EUR-only evaluation. Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported identical aside from a typo) and come from the same publication with the same evaluation ancestry mix and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric).
