Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported string, same method_name PRSCS, same evaluation ancestry and validation sample size, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 with covariates unknown). With endpoint fidelity and study context essentially identical, the only differentiators are the available performance/effect-size signals: PGS005262 shows slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.5933 vs 0.5876) and stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.408 vs 1.362; β 0.342 vs 0.309) than PGS005263. Given the absence of PRS-only metrics, the stronger OR provides the more meaningful tie-break, so PGS005262 is better supported, though confidence is only moderate because differences are small and AUROC is full-model.

Both candidates map cleanly to otosclerosis (trait_efo matches), but PGS002046 provides no PRS-comparable discrimination metrics (only a small partial correlation partial-r=0.0182) whereas PGS001255 reports explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.6319; PGS R2(no covariates)=0.01341), which are directly comparable and pass the heritability sanity-check (well below h2_liability). Although both come from UKB framework-style papers, PGS001255’s endpoint is time-to-event (a mild fidelity penalty vs PGS002046’s generic diagnosis label), yet the presence of clear PGS-only AUC/R2 evidence outweighs PGS002046’s metric sparsity. Covariates are similarly basic in both, so they don’t explain away PGS001255’s PRS-only performance.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported pancreatic cancer; trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident pancreatic cancer), have identical variant count (22), ancestry evaluation (EUR 100%), covariates (including family history and smoking/BMI), and essentially identical reported discrimination/effect size (AUROC 0.745; C-index ~0.742–0.743; HR 1.49). However, PGS000794 is explicitly described as using the same 22 variants from PGS000083 but with inverse variant weights, which is a strong red flag for correctness/biological directionality and suggests it is a derivative/packaging artifact rather than an independently supported PRS. PGS000083 is the original genome-wide significant-variant score from the cross-cancer evaluation with multiple performance records, making it the better-supported record on the visible fields.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported identical aside from spelling) and come from the same publication with the same ancestry distribution, cohort list, and validation sample size, so endpoint fidelity and transportability do not differentiate them. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference is weak evidence; however PGS005262 shows consistently stronger available PRS signal proxies than PGS005261: higher full-model AUROC (0.593 vs 0.585) and, more importantly, a much larger per-SD effect size (OR 1.41 vs 1.05; β 0.34 vs 0.047). Structurally it is also genome-wide (1,085,173 variants; PRSCS) versus a very sparse P+T score (110 variants), which is generally favored for polygenic traits when other fields are equal. Confidence is moderate because covariates are unknown and the only discrimination metric shown is full-model AUROC (not PRS-only).

PGS003385 is less perfectly aligned to the broad target (it is ovarian serous carcinoma rather than generic ovarian neoplasm), but it is still a clinically relevant ovarian cancer subtype endpoint and has a much stronger structural evidence package: a genome-wide lassosum score with 144,810 variants and substantially higher reported discrimination (AUROC 0.717 vs 0.567). Both candidates only report full-model metrics (no PGS-only AUC/R2), so AUC is not cleanly comparable; however, covariates are similarly basic (age+PCs), making the large AUROC gap more credible than in a covariate-heavy setting. By contrast, PGS000549 is an exact broad ovarian malignancy match but is a very sparse GWAS-hits score (16 variants) with weaker reported performance and limited development detail beyond UKB, so overall support favors PGS003385 despite the subtype mismatch.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = malignant neoplasm of ovary; trait_efo = ovarian neoplasm), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (UKB) and training/validation sizes, and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.568 vs 0.567) are essentially noise. Given this near-clone setup, PGS000550 is better-supported because it shows consistently slightly stronger PRS signal in the available comparable evidence: higher per-SD OR (1.286 vs 1.263) and higher pseudo-R² (0.0113 vs 0.00996), and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with far more variants (1,115,189 vs 16 GWAS hits), which is a positive structural tie-break when endpoints/covariates are the same.

PGS000550 is the better match to the target trait (ovarian neoplasm): its trait_efo is exactly "ovarian neoplasm" and phenotyping_reported/trait_reported are the broad malignant ovary cancer endpoint, whereas PGS003385 is explicitly a subtype ("ovarian serous carcinoma") with a different trait_efo, making endpoint fidelity weaker for the umbrella target. Neither record reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher reported AUROC for PGS003385 (0.717) is only a full-model metric and not a reliable cross-model PRS discriminator; additionally, covariates differ (PGS003385 uses 20 PCs vs PGS000550 uses basic age/sex/PCs/batch). With comparable ancestry (EUR-only evaluation) and no PRS-only metrics to separate them, the broader, directly aligned ovarian neoplasm endpoint in PGS000550 outweighs PGS003385’s non-comparable full-model AUROC advantage.

PGS000083 is the better-supported choice for the broad target trait “pancreatic carcinoma” because its endpoint is a direct pancreatic cancer incidence phenotype (trait_efo exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident pancreatic cancer) and it is evaluated in a clearly reported European validation set (EVAL: EUR 100%) with a PRS-relevant effect size (HR per SD 1.49, near the ~1.5 strong-signal threshold). In contrast, PGS002264 is narrower (pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma subtype) and its reported AUROC=0.83 is only a full-model metric with explicitly heavy clinical/risk packaging covariates (diabetes status/onset, age at DM diagnosis, waist circumference, family history, “clinical risk”), making the discrimination less attributable to the PRS and less comparable; it also has evaluation ancestry “Not reported.” Neither model provides PGS-only AUC/R2, so the cleaner covariate context and presence of an effect size favor PGS000083 despite PGS002264 having more variants and a higher full-model AUROC.

PGS000794 is the better-supported choice for the broad target trait “pancreatic carcinoma” because its endpoint is a general pancreatic cancer diagnosis (trait_reported: Pancreatic cancer; phenotyping: incident pancreatic cancer; trait_efo: exocrine pancreatic carcinoma), whereas PGS002264 is restricted to the subtype pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), which is narrower than the target. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS002264 (0.83 vs 0.745) is not a valid PRS-comparable advantage—especially given PGS002264’s explicit clinical-risk packaging/mediator-like covariates around diabetes status/onset and age at DM diagnosis plus family history, which likely inflates full-model discrimination. By contrast, PGS000794 reports a standalone genetic effect size (HR 1.49 per SD) and uses more standard epidemiologic covariates (age/sex/PCs plus BMI/smoking), making its evidence less dominated by a disease-adjacent clinical risk wrapper. Confidence is moderate because both lack clean PRS-only metrics and both include some non-genetic covariates (including family history), limiting direct comparability.

Both candidates match the target trait (Parkinson disease) at trait_reported/trait_efo, but PGS000903 has a cleaner generic PD endpoint (phenotyping_reported: "Parkinson's disease") whereas PGS003763 is explicitly "Incident Parkinson Disease" in a frailty-focused time-to-event context, which is a narrower endpoint for a generic PD target. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC cannot be used as a PRS-comparable metric; however PGS000903 provides additional supportive effect-size evidence (e.g., OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25) and comes from a large disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis with multiple development cohorts and multi-ancestry evaluation, while PGS003763 has no training/development cohort information and only a modest HR (high vs low tertile 1.72) from EUR-only evaluation. Overall, PGS000903 is better supported on endpoint generality and disease-focused evidence package.

PGS003587 is better supported for the target trait preeclampsia because its endpoint fidelity is coherent: although trait_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” both trait_efo is preeclampsia and phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia,” matching the target diagnosis. In contrast, PGS004593 has an exact trait_reported (“Preeclampsia”) and trait_efo match, but its phenotyping_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” which is a more direct endpoint mismatch for preeclampsia. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so metrics don’t separate them; effect sizes are similar and modest (PGS003587 OR 1.2 vs PGS004593 HR 1.16). With comparable basic covariates and similar PRS-CS genome-wide construction, the deciding factor is the stronger phenotype alignment of PGS003587.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Parkinson’s disease), identical basic covariates (PCs 1–5, age, sex), same training cohorts and training N, and the same validation sample size (n=999), so the decision rests on structural and supporting performance evidence. PGS000903 is a genome-wide C+T score with far more variants (1805 vs 90 for PGS000902), which is a positive structural signal when PRS-only metrics are absent for both. It also provides additional supportive effect-size evidence (e.g., OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25 and beta/SE), whereas PGS000902 reports only a full-model AUROC with no additional PRS-discrimination proxies. The small full-model AUROC difference (0.692 vs 0.651) is not PRS-comparable, but it is directionally consistent with PGS000903 being stronger.

Both candidates align to the target trait (Parkinson disease) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so comparable PRS discrimination metrics cannot differentiate them. PGS000902 is better supported structurally and by study context: it is derived from a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis with explicit multi-cohort training/development cohorts listed (23andMe, IPDGC, UKB, etc.) and uses more genome-wide significant variants (90 vs 44). Its reported AUROC (0.651) is full-model and thus not PRS-comparable, but it is at least accompanied by basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and a direct PD phenotype. PGS003763 is from a frailty-focused incident PD analysis with no training/development cohort information and only a tertile HR (1.72) reported, which is less directly comparable as a PRS performance signal. Overall, PGS000902 has the stronger disease-genetics evidence package and clearer development provenance.

Both candidates come from the same Nat Med study, use the same method (PRS-CS), have essentially identical evaluation context (EUR-only evaluation, same validation n=25,582), and share the same phenotyping_reported endpoint (“Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia”) with only basic covariates (maternal age, age^2, PCs), so endpoint fidelity and leakage risk are effectively tied. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, the main differentiator is the available PRS effect size: PGS003586 (reported as Pre-eclampsia) shows a stronger per-SD association (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.24–1.38) than PGS003587 (OR 1.20, 1.14–1.26), indicating better discriminative signal for the target trait. Variant counts are nearly identical and do not outweigh the OR difference.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target peripheral vascular disease because it is a disease-focused PAD score with high endpoint fidelity (trait_efo peripheral arterial disease; phenotyping_reported incident peripheral artery disease) and provides strong PRS signal evidence via an effect size (HR per SD 1.66, 95% CI 1.61–1.71) plus broad multi-ancestry evaluation and large validation (n=304,294) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs). In contrast, PGS001843 comes from a UKB portability framework paper with a vague/unspecified phenotype (peripheral vascular disease, unspecified) and shows very weak PRS-comparable performance (partial-r 0.0151) despite larger training n; its sparse 242-variant construction and framework context are weaker support than the disease-specific multi-cohort evidence in PGS005217. Confidence is moderate because neither candidate reports clean PGS-only AUC/R2, and PGS005217’s reported C-index is full-model rather than PRS-only.

PGS003586 has substantially better endpoint fidelity to the target trait preeclampsia: its phenotyping_reported is "Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia" and trait fields align, whereas PGS004593—despite trait_reported "Preeclampsia"—has phenotyping_reported "Gestational hypertension," a related but non-identical hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. Both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so effect-size and study context matter: PGS003586 shows a stronger per-SD association (OR 1.31 vs HR 1.16 for PGS004593) and provides clearer disease-focused multi-cohort development metadata (multiple listed training/development cohorts and a defined training N), while PGS004593 has missing training/cohort details. PGS004593’s larger validation N does not outweigh the phenotype mismatch and weaker effect-size evidence.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target concept despite a slight label mismatch (peripheral artery disease vs peripheral vascular disease) because its phenotyping is a clear clinical endpoint (incident PAD) and it comes from a disease-focused PAD study with broad multi-cohort development and large multi-ancestry evaluation (n=304,294). It also provides a strong PRS-relevant effect size (HR per SD 1.66), whereas PGS002055 is from a UKB portability framework paper with a vague/unspecified phenotype and only a very small PRS signal reported (partial-r 0.0175). Neither reports clean PGS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint specificity and effect-size evidence in PGS005217 outweigh the exact-but-unspecified label match of PGS002055.

PGS001312 is the better-supported choice for generic psoriasis risk because it matches the target endpoint more directly (phenotyping_reported="Psoriasis") whereas PGS001313 is explicitly time-to-event (phenotyping_reported="TTE psoriasis" / trait_reported="Psoriasis (time-to-event)"), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic disease target. On comparable PRS-only metrics, PGS001312 also performs better (PGS-only AUROC 0.6916; PGS-only R2 0.0523) than PGS001313 (0.6729; 0.0497). Both are otherwise near-clones (same snpnet method, same UKB-only training n=269,704, same basic covariates, same evaluation setup/size), so the decision is driven by endpoint alignment plus the modest but consistent PRS-only performance advantage for PGS001312.

PGS001287 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (AUROC=0.67648; R²=0.0335) with only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and its PRS-only R² is plausibly below the provided liability h² ceiling (0.0735). It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) and a much larger training/validation context. In contrast, PGS000342 has exact endpoint wording (“Psoriatic arthritis”) but provides only a full-model AUROC (0.562) with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R², making its performance less comparable and less informative for standalone PRS quality. The main tradeoff is that PGS001287 comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (a known generalizability risk), so confidence is not high, but the lack of PRS-only metrics and weaker AUROC in PGS000342 leaves PGS001287 as the stronger-supported record overall.

PGS001137 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.573 and PGS-only R2=0.00663 (and these are plausibly below the local h2_obs ceiling), whereas PGS002040 provides no AUROC/R2 and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0276), which is less directly comparable as a PRS discrimination metric. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (both map to EFO retinal detachment; PGS002040’s ‘detachments and defects’ is slightly broader but still on-target). Both are UKB-based framework-style scores, but PGS002040’s stronger method/variant count (LDpred2, 706k variants) is outweighed here by its missing PRS-only AUC/R2, making PGS001137 the more evidentially grounded choice.

PGS001313 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.6729 with CI) and PGS-only R² (0.04966) under basic covariates, whereas PGS002083 provides no AUROC/R² at all and only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0632), which is harder to compare directly as a PRS discrimination metric. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (psoriasis; PGS001313 is time-to-event, which is a mild endpoint mismatch vs the generic target, but still clearly psoriasis). Both are UKB-derived framework/portability-style studies, so study archetype doesn’t differentiate strongly; PGS002083 has more variants and larger training N, but those structural advantages don’t outweigh the lack of PRS-only AUC/R² reporting. Therefore PGS001313 has the cleaner, more directly comparable evidence package.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), same UKB-only training (n=391,124), same covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and the same multi-ancestry evaluation context/validation size, so the decision rests on PRS-comparable performance and structural signals. PGS002055 shows a higher PRS-comparable metric (partial-r 0.0175 vs 0.0151 for PGS001843) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far broader variant coverage (599,514 vs 242), which is generally favorable for polygenic disease architectures when other fields are matched. With no PGS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, these modest but consistent advantages make PGS002055 better supported.

PGS001137 is the better-supported choice because it reports PRS-comparable performance metrics for retinal detachment (explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.573 and PGS-only R²=0.00663), allowing a clean comparison and a heritability sanity check (R² remains below the provided h2_obs ceiling). In contrast, PGS001833 has no AUROC/R²/PGS-only metrics reported (only partial correlation=0.0218), making its predictive performance less directly interpretable for PRS selection despite larger variant count and training N. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (both map to EFO retinal detachment), with PGS001833 slightly broader (“detachments and defects”), but that minor wording advantage does not outweigh the missing PRS-comparable metrics.

Both candidates align to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (same trait_reported/trait_efo), but PGS001791 has cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a PRS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.005929 (and this is plausibly below the trait heritability ceiling), whereas PGS004695 provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 at all (only an HR high-vs-low quintile). Structurally, PGS001791 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS-auto) with 910,439 variants and is developed across many biobanks, while PGS004695 is a sparse 23-SNP genome-wide-significant score from an exposure-focused cohort study with more non-genetic covariate adjustment (education, smoking, pack-years, BMI), making its reported HR less directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Validation sizes are similar and do not outweigh the stronger PRS-only metric support for PGS001791.

PGS001791 is more endpoint-faithful to the target by explicitly modeling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all IPF), which is a clinically specific form of pulmonary fibrosis, and it comes from a multi-biobank global analysis with genome-wide shrinkage (PRS-CS-auto; 910,439 variants) and a very large EUR evaluation sample (n=347,350). Although its PRS-comparable signal is modest (covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only R2=0.005929), it is cleanly reported as PRS-only and is below the heritability ceiling sanity check. PGS001030 has a broader but less specific endpoint (pulmonary fibrosis) and reports stronger PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC=0.6252; PGS R2=0.0142), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB sparse framework (“813 traits” snpnet; 51 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external generalization; its apparent advantage is therefore discounted versus the more disease-focused, genome-wide, multi-cohort score.

Both candidates match the target phenotype cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all psoriasis) and both are UKB-based framework-style scores with basic covariates, so endpoint fidelity and leakage risk are essentially tied. The key differentiator is that PGS001312 reports PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6916 and PGS-only R²=0.0523), whereas PGS002083 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0632) and no PGS-only AUROC/R², making its predictive evidence less directly comparable for PRS quality judging. Although PGS002083 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many more variants and larger training N, the absence of PRS-comparable discrimination metrics lowers support relative to PGS001312’s explicit PGS-only AUC/R².

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/trait_efo (rheumatoid arthritis), same phenotyping_reported (Seropositive RA), same covariates=0 (no clinical leakage signal), same training cohort (UKB), same training n=820, same ancestry distribution and evaluation setup, and same validation sample size (n=90,274). Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo are rheumatoid arthritis; phenotyping_reported is the same: Seropositive RA), share identical training cohort (UKB), training size (n=820), ancestry distribution, covariates=0, and validation sample size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model metrics, which are not ideal for PRS comparison). Given this near-clone context, PGS004163 is better-supported because it shows consistently stronger reported performance/effect-size evidence in the selected European validation record (higher AUROC 0.7469 vs 0.7283; higher R² 0.1376 vs 0.1220; higher OR 2.46 vs 2.37) and it is a MultiPRS ensemble (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) with substantially more variants (778,275 vs 373,627), a structural advantage over the single-score LDpred2.CV sibling when endpoints/covariates are otherwise identical.

PGS000922 is the better-supported choice for generic sarcoidosis because it has direct endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all sarcoidosis) and, crucially, reports PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64282; PGS-only R2=0.01741) with only basic covariates. PGS001030 is better supported for the broad target trait “pulmonary fibrosis” because it matches the umbrella endpoint directly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Pulmonary fibrosis”) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6252; PGS-only R2=0.0142) with only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), allowing heritability-ceiling sanity checking. While PGS001030 comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (a known penalty), the presence of explicit PGS-only metrics and direct pulmonary fibrosis endpoint makes it the stronger-supported record here.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Retinal detachments and defects” mapped to EFO retinal detachment), identical training cohort (UKB), training N (391,124), covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), and the same multi-ancestry evaluation context/validation size, so performance and structural signals decide. Both candidates are near-clones: same schizophrenia endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same method (PRS-CS), same GWAS/evaluation ancestry distribution, same covariates (basic demographics/PCs/platform/batch), and both only report a full-model AUROC=0.6 (no PGS-only AUC/R2), so discrimination evidence is weak and largely non-comparable. With that, the best differentiator is effect size: PGS000133 reports a stronger OR per SD (1.691) than PGS000134 (1.483), indicating stronger PRS signal; the larger variant count and validation N for PGS000134 are secondary/weak tie-breakers here. Hence PGS000133, but confidence is low due to missing PRS-only metrics and very similar records.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match carcinoma in situ of skin), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), identical covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same training cohort (MGI) and same training/validation sizes, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). It also uses a shrinkage-style method (lassosum) with slightly more variants (7 vs 5), which is a mild structural advantage when other fields are matched.

Both candidates come from the same pan-trait UKB framework paper ("across 813 traits"), with identical training cohort (UKB), training N (269,704), evaluation ancestry mix, validation N (67,425), and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), so the key differentiator is endpoint fidelity to generic sarcoidosis. PGS000922 targets a direct sarcoidosis case/control phenotype (phenotyping_reported: "Sarcoidosis"), which better matches the target trait "sarcoidosis" than PGS000923’s time-to-event endpoint (phenotyping_reported: "TTE sarcoidosis"; trait_reported: "Sarcoidosis (time-to-event)")—a mild mismatch for a generic disease target. Although PGS000923 has slightly higher PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6456 vs 0.6428; PGS R2 0.018 vs 0.0174) and more variants (22 vs 12), these differences are small and don’t outweigh the cleaner endpoint match of PGS000922.

Both candidates are near-clones: same schizophrenia endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all schizophrenia), same method (PRS-CS), same ancestry context (GWAS EAS+EUR; EUR-only evaluation), same basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/platform/batch), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC reported, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). Given the domain guidance that small full-model AUC gaps are weak but that within-method higher variant count is a moderate positive signal, PGS000136 is better supported overall despite the larger validation n for PGS000133.

Both candidates match the target endpoint equally well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to carcinoma in situ of skin), use the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and share identical EUR-only training/evaluation context (MGI; training n=6,005; validation n=5,500). Although PGS000469 has a genome-wide variant set (1,119,238) vs 7 variants for PGS000471, the direct empirical validation signals in this same study family favor PGS000471.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity and study context: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (squamous cell carcinoma), same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes, and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Given that, PGS000461 has slightly better full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.599 vs 0.593) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0304 vs 0.0268) and per-SD OR (1.491 vs 1.448), while PGS000463 only edges on top-1% OR (3.74 vs 3.51). The evidence is very close, but the overall metric/effect-size profile marginally favors PGS000461.

Both candidates match the target endpoint equally well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to carcinoma in situ of skin), use the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), same EUR-only training/evaluation context, same training N (6,005) and validation N (5,500), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Given that, the best visible empirical support is the stronger observed validation performance/effect sizes: PGS000470 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.557 vs 0.524), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0154 vs 0.00141), stronger per-SD OR (1.308 vs 1.09), and stronger top-1% vs rest OR (2.45 vs 1.48). Although PGS000469 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method with many variants, its reported discrimination/effect sizes are materially weaker here, so PGS000470 is better supported on the available record fields.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity for the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to thyroid cancer/thyroid carcinoma), come from the same publication and training cohort (MGI; n=4,481), use the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and have the same validation sample size (n=4,270), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either record (only full-model metrics). Given that, small full-model AUROC/R2 differences are weak, but PGS000630 shows slightly better full-model AUROC (0.626 vs 0.618) and pseudo-R² (0.0393 vs 0.0365) and uses more variants (10 vs 8). PGS000632 has a higher top-1% OR (5.14 vs 3.53), but overall the evidence is near-tied and based on non-PRS-only metrics, so confidence is low.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (squamous cell carcinoma), same publication and release date, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training N (8,029), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation N (8,473). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC differences are only weakly informative. With endpoints and covariates effectively identical, PGS000461 has slightly stronger overall discrimination evidence (full-model AUROC 0.599 vs 0.589; Nagelkerke R² 0.0304 vs 0.0282) and a marginally higher per-SD OR (1.491 vs 1.457), while PGS000465’s only standout is a higher top-1% vs rest OR (4.54 vs 3.51). Given the lack of PRS-only metrics and the mixed effect-size signals, the edge to PGS000461 is small, hence low confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target trait/phenotyping (schizophrenia), same EFO mapping, same method (PRS-CS), very similar variant counts, identical covariates (basic demographics/PCs/platform/batch; no obvious leakage), and same ancestry context (GWAS mostly EUR with small EAS; EUR-only evaluation). With no PGS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (only full-model AUROC), the main differentiator is the available effect-size and full-model discrimination: PGS000136 shows higher AUROC (0.64 vs 0.60) and stronger OR per SD (1.7 vs 1.483) than PGS000134. Although PGS000134 has a larger validation N (44,436 vs 18,461), validation size is a weak tie-breaker and does not outweigh the consistently stronger performance/effect-size signals in PGS000136.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match squamous cell carcinoma), come from the same publication, use the same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, identical training (n=8,029) and validation size (n=8,473), and have similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.593 for PGS000463 vs 0.589 for PGS000465) are not a strong differentiator. With endpoints and covariates effectively identical, PGS000465 has slightly stronger PRS signal in the available effect-size summaries (top 1% vs rest OR 4.54 vs 3.74; per-SD OR 1.457 vs 1.448) and a higher variant count (10 vs 7), making it marginally better supported despite the different method labels.

Both candidates have identical endpoint alignment to the target (trait_reported/efo = rheumatoid arthritis; phenotyping_reported = Seropositive RA), identical covariates (0), identical training cohort and size (UKB; n=820), and identical ancestry/validation context. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we must rely on the available full-model metrics/effect sizes and structural signals. PGS004163 shows consistently stronger reported performance than PGS004079 in the selected European validation record (higher AUROC 0.747 vs 0.719; higher R² 0.138 vs 0.113; higher OR per SD 2.46 vs 2.22), and it also has a larger variant count (778,275 vs 402,214) with an ensemble-style method name (MultiPRS) versus a single-method MegaPRS. Given otherwise near-clone metadata, these advantages make PGS004163 better supported.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate Type 1 diabetes). However, PGS001297 provides PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.771 and PGS-only R²=0.0912) with clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), allowing a cleaner assessment of the genetic score contribution and passing the heritability-ceiling sanity check (R² well below h2_liability~0.219). In contrast, PGS000024 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.921) with covariates listed as unknown and no PGS-only AUROC/R², so its apparently high discrimination is not comparable and could be covariate-driven; despite being disease-focused and having broader evaluation ancestry/large validation N, the lack of PRS-only metrics makes it less well-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to thyroid cancer/thyroid carcinoma), use the same GWAS Hits method with 10 variants, and have similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4) with no obvious leakage. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so only full-model metrics and effect sizes are available and are weak differentiators. PGS000631 has slightly stronger reported discrimination/effect evidence (full-model AUROC 0.636 vs 0.626; per-SD OR 1.651 vs 1.598; top 1% OR 4.4 vs 3.53), while PGS000630 has broader evaluation ancestry (EUR+MAE) and larger training/validation Ns. Given the same endpoint and covariates, the modestly stronger effect-size/AUROC signals favor PGS000631, but the trade-offs make confidence low.

PGS000923 is the better-supported match to the target trait sarcoidosis because its concept alignment is coherent across fields (trait_efo="sarcoidosis" and phenotyping_reported="TTE sarcoidosis"), whereas PGS001872 maps to a narrower/different concept (trait_efo="skin sarcoidosis") despite a generic phenotyping_reported label. PGS000923 also reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64561 and PGS-only R2=0.018), enabling direct PRS evaluation and a heritability-ceiling sanity check; PGS001872 lacks AUROC/R2 and only provides partial correlation (partial-r=0.0199), which is less directly comparable. Both are UKB framework-style scores with basic covariates and similar multi-ancestry evaluation strings, so the decision is driven mainly by stronger endpoint fidelity to general sarcoidosis plus clearer PRS-only metrics for PGS000923.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity for the target (trait_efo thyroid carcinoma; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Thyroid cancer”), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use PRS-comparable discrimination; only full-model AUROC/R2 and effect sizes are visible. Given that, PGS000631 has slightly better full-model AUROC (0.636 vs 0.618) and higher per-SD OR (1.651 vs 1.568), while PGS000632’s advantages are larger training/validation sample sizes and a higher top-1% OR (5.14 vs 4.4). With metrics largely non-comparable and differences modest, I favor PGS000631 on the more general discrimination signals (AUROC and per-SD OR), but confidence is low because both are near-clone records and rely on full-model metrics.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo and trait_reported are T1D; phenotyping_reported is direct T1D in both). However, PGS001297 provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.771 and PGS-only R²=0.0912 with basic covariates listed), which can be sanity-checked against the trait heritability ceiling and directly compared across models. In contrast, PGS004162 reports only full-model AUROC/R² (no PGS-only AUC/R²) so its discrimination is not comparable as a standalone PRS metric, despite having many more variants and reporting effect sizes. Given the policy that full-model AUROC should not substitute for PRS-only performance, PGS001297 is better-supported on the visible evidence.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), so phenotype and leakage concerns don’t separate them. The key difference is PRS-comparable performance evidence: PGS001306 reports explicit PGS-only metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.63006; PGS R2(no covariates)=0.02036), which are interpretable and below the heritability ceiling, whereas PGS004253 reports no PGS-only AUC/R2 and only a full-model AUROC=0.66 (not comparable as a standalone PRS metric). Although PGS004253 provides a strong OR per SD (1.84) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with many variants, the lack of PRS-only discrimination metrics makes its support weaker on the visible fields than PGS001306’s directly comparable PRS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use comparable PRS discrimination metrics. PGS004253 has stronger PRS-specific evidence via an effect size (OR=1.84 per SD, 95% CI 1.76–1.93), which is a strong discriminative signal, and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with very large variant count (LDpred2-auto; 744,575 variants) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array). PGS001855 comes from a UKB portability framework paper with a very sparse model (1,505 variants) and only a modest partial correlation (partial-r=0.0625) as its main performance evidence; despite broader evaluation ancestries and larger training/validation N, that framework/sparse signature is a negative generalization signal relative to the disease-focused UC score with strong OR evidence.

Both candidates align well to the target trait (trait_efo is type 1 diabetes mellitus; phenotyping_reported is T1D/Type 1 diabetes). However, PGS000024 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.921) with covariates listed as Unknown and provides no PRS-only AUROC/R² or effect sizes, making its apparent performance hard to attribute to the PRS itself. PGS004162 also lacks explicit PRS-only metrics, but it has cleaner disclosed covariates (covariates=0), provides uncertainty-bounded performance (AUROC with CI and R² with CI) plus effect sizes (OR and β), and uses a genome-wide/ensemble-style score with many variants (62,645 vs 85), which is a supportive structural signal when PRS-only metrics are absent. Therefore PGS004162 is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target well (same trait_reported, trait_efo, and phenotyping_reported) and have similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4) with EUR-only training/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC ~0.57 is not a strong differentiator). PGS000613 is better supported structurally and by effect-size evidence: it uses P+T with slightly more variants (15 vs 13), has a larger training sample (12,992 vs 7,469), a much stronger top-1% vs rest OR (2.91 vs 1.47, with tighter/clearly >1 CI), and a slightly better Brier score (0.0821 vs 0.0917). PGS000610’s marginally higher full-model AUROC/R2 is negligible given both are full-model metrics and near-identical.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported "Cancer of bladder", same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort UKB and training n=12,992, same covariates age/sex/batch/PCs1-4, same validation n=13,530) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, so limited comparability). Given identical endpoint fidelity and covariate cleanliness, PGS000613 has consistently slightly stronger reported validation signals than PGS000611: higher AUROC (0.571 vs 0.567), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0125 vs 0.0114), higher top-1% OR (2.91 vs 2.66), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.301 vs 1.284), with a modestly larger variant set (15 vs 13). The differences are small, so confidence is moderate.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Ulcerative colitis”) and similarly basic covariates (no family history/biomarker/risk-calculator packaging). The key differentiator is performance evidence: PGS001306 reports PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.63006 and PGS-only R²=0.02036), which are interpretable and below the heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.2646), whereas PGS001855 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0625) and no PRS-only AUROC/R², making cross-model PRS discrimination comparison weaker. Although PGS001855 has more variants (1505 vs 179) and larger training N, those are secondary to having clean, directly comparable PRS-only metrics, so PGS001306 is better supported on the visible fields.

PGS002075 is the better-supported choice for the target trait urolithiasis because its endpoint is a direct, generic diagnosis-aligned phenotype (“Urinary calculus” with trait_efo=urolithiasis) and it is built as a genome-wide shrinkage score (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (731,196) and explicit multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS), which is supportive for transportability. PGS001250 does report clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.5668; PGS R2 0.00592), but it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (341 variants) and uses a time-to-event phenotype (“TTE calculus of kidney and ureter”), which is a mild endpoint packaging mismatch for a generic urolithiasis target. Given PGS002075’s stronger endpoint fidelity and more robust model structure despite missing PRS-only AUC/R2, it edges out PGS001250.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported, same method and 13 variants, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, and same basic covariates), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC), so performance is not cleanly comparable. PGS000610 has a trivially higher full-model AUROC (0.572 vs 0.567) but also a worse top-1% OR (1.47 vs 2.66) and worse Brier score (0.0917 vs 0.0821). With endpoints/covariates essentially identical, the stronger risk-stratification signal favors PGS000611; training/validation size differences (UKB n=12,992/13,530 vs MGI n=7,469/7,622) are weak tie-breakers. Confidence is low because the key PRS-only metrics are missing and the AUROC differences are small.

PGS001250 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence for urolithiasis: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.5668; PGS R2 0.00592) in Europeans, whereas PGS001864 provides only a small partial correlation (partial-r 0.0323) and has no AUC/R2 fields populated. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (PGS001864: “Urinary calculus” mapped to urolithiasis; PGS001250: “Calculus of kidney and ureter” time-to-event mapped to nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis), with PGS001250 having a mild penalty for the time-to-event framing but still clearly within the same disease spectrum. Both are UKB-based framework/portability-style scores with basic covariates, so study archetype does not differentiate strongly; given that, the presence of clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 in PGS001250 outweighs PGS001864’s missing comparable metrics despite PGS001864’s larger variant count and broader listed evaluation ancestries.

PGS001795 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a PRS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2 of 0.001948, which is interpretable as PRS signal and is below the uterine-cancer heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0116), whereas PGS000541 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 and only a full-model AUROC (0.576) that is not comparable as a standalone PRS metric. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (uterine cancer/uterine carcinoma vs malignant neoplasm of uterus), and both use only basic demographic/PC covariates, but PGS001795 also has a much larger external evaluation sample (n=170,276 vs n=6,987), increasing trust in the reported metrics. Despite PGS000541’s reported OR per SD (~1.31) and clean covariates, the lack of PRS-only metrics makes it less well-supported than PGS001795 in this head-to-head.

PGS001536 is better supported for vitiligo because it has clear endpoint alignment (trait_efo=Vitiligo; phenotyping_reported explicitly “TTE vitiligo”) and, crucially, reports PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193 and PGS-only R2=0.01621) with only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs). Its PRS-only R2 is also plausible under the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.17). In contrast, PGS000738 has a major phenotype/endpoint incoherence: phenotyping_reported is “Red hair,” which does not match vitiligo, and it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a pseudo R²/full-model-style metric is shown), making its predictive evidence much less comparable despite the disease-focused publication title.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Urinary calculus”, trait_efo urolithiasis), study context (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), and evaluation setup (same multi-ancestry distribution; selected European validation; n=19,913). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the only comparable performance signal shown is partial correlation, where PGS002075 is higher (partial-r 0.0385 vs 0.0323 for PGS001864). Structurally, PGS002075 also uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (731,196 vs 5,599), which is a positive tie-break for a polygenic disease when other fields are matched. Hence PGS002075 is better supported overall.

PGS001536 is endpoint-aligned to the target trait (phenotyping_reported: "TTE vitiligo"; trait_reported: "Vitiligo (time-to-event)") and provides PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.64193; PGS-only R2 0.01621), which are cleanly interpretable and below the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.17). It also uses only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs) and shows multi-ancestry evaluation. In contrast, PGS000760 has a clear phenotype mismatch (phenotyping_reported: "anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients"), lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 entirely (only a meta-analysis p-value and an HR), and is effectively treatment-context specific rather than vitiligo risk prediction. These differences make PGS001536 much better supported for vitiligo.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity for the target (uterine cancer): PGS000542 uses “Malignant neoplasm of uterus” and PGS001795 uses “Uterine cancer/uterine carcinoma,” with matching phenotyping_reported fields. The key differentiator is PRS-comparable performance evidence and model structure: PGS001795 reports a PRS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2 of 0.001948, which is an explicitly PRS-comparable metric and is below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0116), making it interpretable. In contrast, PGS000542 provides only full-model AUROC/R2 (AUROC 0.572) without a PRS-only metric, so its discrimination is not cleanly attributable to the PRS. Structurally, PGS001795 is genome-wide (911,692 variants; PRS-CS-auto) versus PGS000542’s very sparse 20-variant P+T score, which is generally weaker for polygenic traits. Although PGS001795 comes from a global biobank framework-style paper and uses heavier but still basic demographic/PC covariates, the presence of an explicit PRS-comparable R2 and the much stronger genome-wide construction outweigh PGS000542’s sparse model with only full-model metrics.

PGS000738 is the better-supported vitiligo PRS because its evidence is at least tied on trait label (both have Vitiligo / EFO Vitiligo) but substantially cleaner on endpoint fidelity: its validation is presented as vitiligo in a vitiligo-focused study context, whereas PGS000760’s phenotyping_reported is explicitly treatment/setting-specific (“anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients”), which is not a direct vitiligo endpoint and suggests a therapy-induced/oncology-context phenotype mismatch. On performance evidence, neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, but PGS000738 provides an actual validation pseudo-R² (0.0386), while PGS000760 provides only a meta-analysis p-value plus an HR (1.41) tied to the non-vitiligo phenotype context, making its PRS discriminative evidence less comparable for vitiligo risk. Both are EUR-only evaluation; although PGS000760 lists a large training sample (UKB, n=408,959), training N is a weak differentiator and does not compensate for the endpoint mismatch. Therefore PGS000738 is preferred.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (malignant neoplasm of uterus/uterine cancer), same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (UKB) and size (n=7,131), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation size (n=6,987). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot compare clean PRS metrics and must treat full-model AUROC differences as weak. On the available evidence, PGS000541 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.576 vs 0.572) and slightly higher pseudo-R² (0.0133 vs 0.0126) and per-SD OR (1.311 vs 1.302), while PGS000542 only has a higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.6 vs 2.12). Given the minimal, mixed differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, the edge is marginal, but PGS000541 is slightly more consistently better across the general discrimination/effect-size fields.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target trait (kidney cancer) because it is derived from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet; BBJ/FinnGen/NCI) and shows a much stronger PRS effect size (OR 1.5 per SD, 95% CI 1.43–1.58) than PGS000076 (HR 1.16, 1.08–1.26), suggesting materially stronger genetic discrimination. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (PGS004908: kidney cancer/renal carcinoma; PGS000076: incident kidney cancer/renal cell carcinoma—dominant subtype), and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.74 vs 0.722) are not decisive. With similar covariate heaviness, the stronger effect size and disease-focused GWAS support favor PGS004908 over the older cross-cancer evaluation score PGS000076.
